paper.title: The Role of Bequests in Shaping Wealth Inequality: Evidence from Danish Wealth Records
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement beyond the article page: …

variables_mentioned: aggregate value of asset holdings and liabilities
cash value of property assessed by the tax agency

linkages: Population registers enable linking individuals born in 1960 and onward to their parents
Standard errors clustered by parents, who may have more than one child

sample.universe: Danish individuals born 1960 and onward who can be linked to their parents; children aged 45-50 in 2010 with a single living biological parent in 2009
selection_rules: children between 45 and 50 years old in 2010, so that parents are observed in the data
restrict attention to those with a single living biological parent in 2009, so that parental death corresponds to the flow of bequests to children rather than to a surviving spouse
treatment group: parent dies in 2010; control group: parent remains alive
control group reweighted to match, for each child cohort, the percentile distribution of parental wealth (average wealth 2003-2009) in the treatment group
sample.n_individuals: 6,252 in the treatment group and 148,166 in the control group

construction_notes: Wealth = aggregate value of asset holdings and liabilities at the end of the year, based mainly on third-party reports to the Danish tax agency; pension wealth is not included
Registered housing values scaled up by the average ratio of actual house prices to assessed values for houses sold 2003-2013, a scaling factor of 1.16, following Leth-Petersen (2010)
Wealth distributions censored at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles for each group in each year (main results); the top 1 percent analysed separately
Percentile ranks of parents calculated within each child cohort based on average wealth seven years before death (2003-2009)
Confidence intervals in Tables 1 and 2 from 1,000 bootstrap replications clustered by parents

claims.statement: Receipt of bequests following parental death raises the average wealth of children by DKK 127,130, about 36 percent of the control-group average.

treatment.label: Receipt of bequests following death of the parent in 2010 (treatment vs. control group)

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark population registers (linking individuals born in 1960 and onward to their parents); no register codes or variable names are given

definition.value: Death of the parent in 2010 (treatment group) versus a parent still alive (control group); the paper does not observe inheritances directly but treats the flow of bequests following parental death as the treatment. Sample restricted to children with a single living biological parent in 2009, so parental death corresponds to the flow of bequests to children rather than to a surviving spouse.

timing.value: Parental death occurs in 2010; wealth compared between 2008 (pre) and 2011 (post)

outcome.label: Average wealth of the child (censored at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles)

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark wealth registers (aggregate value of asset holdings and liabilities of each individual at the end of the year); no variable codes named

definition.value: Mean of the individual end-of-year net wealth distribution (assets minus liabilities, housing scaled up by 1.16), censored at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles for each group and year; Wealth distributions are censored at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles for each group in each year; all amounts in 2010 DKK ($1 = DKK 5.6); control group reweighted to match, for each child cohort, the percentile distribution of parental wealth in the treatment group.

timing.value: End-of-year wealth of the child in 2011, one year after parental death (compared with 2008)

units.value: 2010 DKK (difference in average wealth, treatment minus control, 2011 versus 2008)

magnitude.interpretation: bequests on average increase wealth by 36 percent; bequests account for 26 percent (=0.36/1.36) of overall wealth of the treatment group

estimand.target_population: Children aged 45-50 in 2010 whose single living biological parent died in 2010 in Denmark
estimand.time_horizon: one year after parental death (2011 versus 2008 comparison)

key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 shows almost no difference between treatment and control groups in the years preceding parental death; the paper states the parallel trends assumption is consistent with the data

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample construction; online Appendix displays average parental wealth in treatment vs. control before and after reweighting

implies_edges.from: parental wealth rank (2003-2009) and child cohort

key_assumptions.assumption: The post-death change in child wealth reflects the flow of bequests (and closely related transfers/expenditures) rather than other consequences of parental death
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes the analysis accounts not only for bequests but also for other wealth transfers taking place shortly before death and expenditures of children related to parental deaths

threats_discussed: Time of death is related to socioeconomic status, so parental (and child) wealth is lower in the treatment group; addressed by reweighting the control group on parental wealth percentiles
Pre-death wealth transfers to avoid the bequest tax may show up before the year of death
Over time, parents in the control group are also beginning to die
Assessed housing values are below market values; scaled up by a factor 1.16 following Leth-Petersen (2010)
robustness_checks: Results without censoring the distribution at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles (average effect 34 percent; bequests account for 25 percent of wealth)
Online Appendix: same cohorts but deaths in 2007 (children 42-47), compared with a control group whose parent is alive in 2013, followed up to six years after death
Online Appendix: average parental wealth in treatment vs. control before and after reweighting
unresolved_confounders: The data do not include information on pension wealth
Inheritances are not observed directly
